items.title: How a 66-Year-Old’s $800,000 in JEPQ and QQQI Pays $8,200 a Month, and the IRS Only Sees Half of It
items.summary: An $800,000 split between two Nasdaq-100 income ETFs generates a stunning monthly payout, but the tax bill tells a completely different story than the distribution notices suggest.
items.text:
How a 66-Year-Old’s $800,000 in JEPQ and QQQI Pays $8,200 a Month, and the IRS Only Sees Half of It
An $800,000 split between two Nasdaq-100 income ETFs generates a stunning monthly payout, but the tax bill tells a completely different story than the distribution notices suggest.
A 66-year-old with $800,000 split evenly between two Nasdaq-100 income ETFs watches roughly $8,240 hit the account every month. Only about $3,565 of that shows up on this year’s tax return. The rest looks like income and spends like income, but it quietly comes out of the investor’s own cost basis.
What $800,000 in JEPQ and QQQI Actually Pays
The setup is simple: JPMorgan Nasdaq Equity Premium Income ETF (NASDAQ:JEPQ) at $400,000, NEOS Nasdaq-100 High Income ETF (NASDAQ:QQQI) at $400,000. JEPQ threw off a trailing 12-month total of $6.76 per share and shows an annualized forward run rate of $8.19. QQQI’s trailing 12-month distributions total $7.65 per share, with a forward figure of $7.82. Split the portfolio in half, and the headline math works out to roughly $42,760 from JEPQ plus $56,120 from QQQI, or $98,880 a year.
Why the IRS Sees Less Than Half
This is where the “IRS only sees half” angle comes from. JEPQ generates most of its yield by selling calls through equity-linked notes; those payouts land as ordinary income, taxed at the retiree’s marginal rate. QQQI works differently. Its distributions are dominated by return of capital. NEOS filed Form 8937 disclosing that FY2025 QQQI distributions were classified as nontaxable return of capital under IRC Section 301(c)(2), which reduces shareholder cost basis rather than triggering a current tax liability. The reported ROC percentages ran from 94.45% on early payments up to 98.86% on the spring 2025 distributions.
At roughly 99% ROC, only about $224 of the $56,120 QQQI stream is currently taxable. Combined with JEPQ’s ordinary-income payout, the retiree reports somewhere near 43% of the $98,880 as current-year income. The other 57% is a tax-deferred cash flow — the tax is deferred until shares are sold or the estate is settled. Every ROC dollar shrinks the cost basis in QQQI, so the eventual sale (or the death step-up window) becomes the taxable event.
Fees Paid Before the First Dollar of Income
Both funds quietly charge more than a plain Nasdaq-100 index tracker. JEPQ’s expense ratio sits at 0.35% and QQQI’s at 0.68%. Translated to dollars: $35 per $10,000 per year in JEPQ, $68 per $10,000 per year in QQQI. On this $800,000 split, that is roughly $4,120 in annual fees. The same money in Invesco NASDAQ 100 ETF (NASDAQ:QQQM) at 0.15% would run about $1,200. Over 20 years, that gap alone — before any compounding — is roughly $58,400 handed to the fund issuers.
Two Tickers, One Bet
The diversification is largely cosmetic. JEPQ’s largest positions include NVIDIA at 6.59% of net assets, Apple at 5.74%, Micron at 5.50%, Alphabet at 4.98%, Microsoft at 3.84%, AMD at 3.81%, and Amazon at 3.62%. QQQI’s top holdings include NVIDIA at 7.65%, Apple at 6.63%, Micron at 5.61%, Microsoft at 4.38%, AMD at 4.12%, Amazon at 4.05%, and Tesla at 3.35%. The retiree owns the same names twice, pays two active-fund fees for the privilege, and caps upside on both sides through short-call overlays.
A Cheaper Mirror With the Same Stocks
For pure Nasdaq-100 exposure, Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) at 0.18% or QQQM at 0.15% own the same mega-caps without an options overlay and without ELN counterparty exposure. The trade-off is real: distribution yield drops from double digits to roughly 0.5%, so an income-focused retiree would need to sell shares periodically to replicate the $8,240 monthly draw. In exchange, nothing caps appreciation in a strong rally, and no ROC quietly depletes basis. For reference, JEPQ is up 10.63% year-to-date and QQQI is up 10.36%, both trailing what a plain Nasdaq-100 fund captured over the same period.
What This Means for You
Ask three questions before you commit to a double-digit yield: How much of that payout is actually income, how much is principal being handed back to you, and what would a portfolio at 0.15% total cost in the same underlying stocks look like after 20 years? A distribution that leans heavily on return of capital is one of the classic tells we cover in a free guide to dividend traps. The IRS may only see half today. The retiree eventually sees all of it.

items.title: 1 Popular Cryptocurrency Cathie Wood of Ark Invest Sees Soaring in Value by 1,490%
items.summary: Wood has some very high hopes for Bitcoin.
items.text:
Cathie Wood, founder and CEO of Ark Invest, has been an outspoken proponent of Bitcoin (BTC -0.08%) for many years. Investors who follow Wood can gain exposure to Bitcoin through her company's ARK 21Shares Bitcoin ETF (ARKB +0.16%), and her latest estimates of where the cryptocurrency will be in just five years are bullish, to say the least.
Wood said earlier this year that the base case for Bitcoin's price is $750,000 and its bull case could see it rising to $1.25 million.
With one Bitcoin worth about $78,442 as of this writing, Wood's bull case would see Bitcoin rising a staggering 1,490% over the next five years.
Here's why Wood is so optimistic about Bitcoin's rise -- and why she's probably overestimating where it's headed.
Why Cathie Wood thinks Bitcoin could reach $1.25 million
In a Fox News interview back in April, Wood highlighted a handful of catalysts that will push Bitcoin higher. And one of the most important drivers of its price, according to her, is continued institutional adoption.
She said that institutions are increasingly adding Bitcoin to their portfolios and that, as they continue to do so, it will help boost the cryptocurrency's price. She's not wrong that Bitcoin has gained widespread popularity among financial institutions. Since spot Bitcoin ETFs were launched in 2024, they collectively have $102 billion in assets under management.
More financial institutions could adopt Bitcoin investing in the future, too. The CLARITY Act is currently under consideration in Congress and would create a clear federal regulatory framework for cryptocurrencies. If it passes, it could convince even more financial institutions to give their customers access to buying and selling Bitcoin, which could drive its price higher.
Wood also believes that a generational wealth transfer and more investors using Bitcoin as a substitute for gold will drive its value up. She said that as younger people inherit wealth in the coming years, they'll be more inclined to put some of it into Bitcoin and other digital assets.
CRYPTO: BTC
Key Data Points
Is Bitcoin at $1.25 million realistic?
In a word, no.
For one, Bitcoin's value has increased over the past several years because of the launch of Bitcoin ETFs. But much of that momentum has already run its course. It's already easy for investors to buy and sell crypto through ETFs, so even if the CLARITY Act passes and more financial institutions dip their toes into Bitcoin, it's unlikely to create enough momentum to significantly increase its value.
I also think there's a shift in investor perspectives right now, as people realize they can earn significant returns by investing in highly profitable AI stocks -- without the risks associated with cryptocurrencies.
As long as AI stocks are booming and tech companies are delivering impressive profits, there's less incentive to invest in Bitcoin and other cryptos that don't have real products or services, don't have earnings, and carry far more risk.
I don't think investors should avoid Bitcoin, especially if they want to diversify their portfolios. But expecting its value to soar 1,490% over the next five years just doesn't seem realistic.
